abstract: Significance As one of newly uncovered posttranslational modifications, histone lysine lactylation (Kla) has been shown to exert a critical role in fundamental processes. But how this mark mediates downstream effects remains unclear owing to the lack of its reader proteins. Leveraging a multivalent photoaffinity probe coupled with quantitative proteomics, we identified DPF2 as a bona fide effector of H3K14la. Subsequently, DPF2 was verified to be recruited to gene promoters via recognition with Histone Kla, leading to modulation of transcription. This work described an epigenetic reader for histone Kla, which paves the way for further functional dissections of this mark.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Materials.
Deacetylase inhibitor Cocktail (100X) (P1112) was obtained from Beyotime and protease inhibitor cocktail (100X) (C0001) was obtained from Roche. Primary antibodies were obtained from PTM BIO [Kla (PTM-1401RM), H3K14ac (PTM-113RM), H3K14la (PTM-1414RM), H3K9la (PTM-1419RM), H3K18la (PTM-1406RM), H4K5la (PTM-1407RM), H4K8la (PTM-1415RM)], Cell Signaling Technology [Histone H3, (96C10)], and Sigma-Aldrich [FLAG M2, (F3165)]. Sodium L-lactate (71718) and sodium oxamate (O2751) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Histone peptides with and without lysine lactylation (Kla) modification were synthesized and HPLC purified by Beijing SciLight Biotechnology Ltd. Co. Thiolated polyethylene glycol (HS-PEG) modified with benzophenone (HS-PEG-Bpa) was obtained from ToYong Biotech Ltd. AuNPs was purchased from BBI solutions. HPLC solvents used for mass spectrometric analysis of proteins were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific Ltd.
Enrichment of Endogenous Binding Proteins using Probe H3K14la.
Briefly, 2 mM H3K14la peptides and 1 mM HS-PEG-Bpa were mixed and added to the solution of gold nanoparticles (200 μL), and the mixture was shaken at room temperature for 12 h. Then, the functionalized gold nanoparticles were washed with H
2
O (50 μL) twice and then the fabricated probes were stored at 4 °C for further use. For comparison, probe H3K14 was developed accordingly. The functionalized probes H3K14la and H3K14 were, respectively, incubated with 0.5 mg of nuclear extracts for 12 h at 4 °C in a rotation wheel. Then, the mixture was irradiated at 365 nm on ice for 20 min using UVP Crosslinker (Analytik Jena). After centrifugation, the precipitation was washed twice with wash buffer 1 (4 M urea in PBS), followed by once washing with buffer 2 (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 200 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM ZnCl
2
) and one wash with wash buffer 3 (100 mM NH
4
HCO
3
). Next, the pellet was suspended in 50 μL NH
4
HCO
3
(100 mM) and digested with trypsin at 37 °C overnight. The resulting solution was centrifuged for 2 min and the supernatant was collected. Then, 5 mM DTT was added and incubated with the obtained solution for 1 h, followed by reaction with 15 mM iodoacetamide and 30 mM cysteine at room temperature. The resulting peptide mixture was desalted with C18 material and further analyzed by HPLC-MS/MS.
Immunofluorescence Assay.
For immunofluorescent staining, cells were grown on chamber slides, washed in PBS, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. After fixing, the cells were then permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS, blocked by 10% normal goat serum (NGS), and then incubated with anti-FLAG (F3165, Sigma-Aldrich) and H3K14la (PTM-1414RM, PTMBio) antibodies for 12 h at 4 °C. Next, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor–conjugated secondary antibodies for 1.5 h in room temperature. Finally, the cells were counterstained with DAPI and imaged using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (Zeiss LSM 900). All images were subsequently analyzed using ImageJ.
CUT&Tag.
CUT&Tag was performed using the Hyperactive Universal CUT&Tag Assay Kit for Illumina (TD903, Vazyme Biotech) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, HeLa cells expressing Flag-WT-DPF2 or its mutants, and cells expressing Flag-WT-BAF47 were collected and counted for incubation with pre-coated concanavalin A beads. Subsequently, cells were permeabilized by digitonin and incubated with Flag or H3K14la antibodies. Next, the samples were incubated with pA-Tn5 transposase. After transposon activation and tagmentation, DNA was isolated, amplified, and purified to construct library. The samples were then analyzed on an Illumina NovaSeq 150PE platform.
RNA-seq Analysis.
Total RNA was extracted from HeLa cells by TRIzol (Invitrogen) and were then sequenced using the Illumina Hiseq 2500. The raw reads were mapped to the human reference genome (hg19) and transcriptome using the RNA-Seq unified mapper. Read counts for each transcript were calculated using HTseq v0.6.1 using default parameters 54. Differential gene expression analyses were performed using the “exactTest” function in edgeR v3.055.
Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) Assay.
CCK-8 was used to measure cell proliferation. HeLa cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 2,000 cells per well. After adhesion, the cells were treated with 20 mM sodium lactate or 20 mM sodium oxamate. Every 24 h for 7 d, 10 μL of the CCK-8 solution was added to each well with incubation for 2 h at 37 °C. The absorbance of each well was then measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek). Finally, the numbers of living cells over 7 d were plotted in a graph to calculate the cell proliferation rate.

body:
Histone posttranslational modifications (hPTMs) are crucial epigenetic marks that provide fine-tuned mechanisms for regulating diverse biological events such as chromatin structure and dynamic, transcription, and DNA damage repair (
1
–
3
). In addition to the well-studied acetylation and methylation, recent studies have revealed several new types of histone lysine modifications, including crotonylation (Kcr) (
4
), succinylation (Ksucc) (
5
), 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) (
6
), β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb) (
7
), and lactylation (Kla) (
8
). These marks are typically decorated on the histone tails and proposed to contribute gene expression program by either influencing histone–DNA interactions or recruiting specific protein effectors (also referred to as histone readers) (
9
–
11
). Since the first discovery of bromodomain (BrD) as a reader of histone acetylation (
12
), a growing number of effectors have been found for specific recognition of the mark (
13
–
15
). However, the reader proteins responsible for the readout of the different histone marks such as lactylation remain largely unknown.
Histone lactylation is a recently uncovered hPTM that renders a link between cellular metabolism and epigenetic regulatory mechanisms (
8
). It is proposed to be stimulated by intracellular metabolite-lactate that derived from enhanced glycolysis known as the Warburg effect found in cancers (
16
–
18
). Notably, hypoxia as well as macrophage polarization both contribute to increased histone lactylation enriched at specific genes, bolstering the evidence that this mark is metabolically induced and leads to distinct transcriptional outcomes from acetylation (
19
). Indeed, Yu and coworkers (
20
) observed that histone lactylation drives oncogenesis by promoting YTHDF2 (m
6
A reader protein) expression in ocular melanoma, providing novel understanding of epigenetic regulation in tumorigenesis. Besides, Yuan group demonstrated a glycolysis–H4K12la–PKM2 positive feedback loop in microglia that facilitates the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) (
21
), expanding the role of histone lactylation. Similarly, Rho et al. (
22
) reported that HK2-induced gene expression via histone lactylation governs hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis. Recently, Merkuri and others showed that histone lactylation integrates cellular metabolism with developmental gene networks orchestrated embryonic development (
23
). However, how histone lactylation functions in the transcriptional regulation of the specific genes associated with biological events is poorly understand. Considering that the recognition of hPTMs by readers is capable of mediating specific gene transcription and biological consequences in a high context-dependent manner (
24
–
26
), the interpreting of effectors reading histone lactylation is key to understanding the mechanism underlying in epigenetic regulatory pathways.
Deciphering the hPTM protein effectors is still a challenge due to the facts that the interactions between hPTMs and its binding proteins are typically weak, transient, and dynamic (
27
–
29
). Thus, current methods relying on peptide-based affinity pulldowns may not be suitable for this end, whereas photo-cross-linking could be employed as an alternative strategy to capture hPTM binders by converting noncovalent binding to covalent linkages (
30
,
31
). We recently developed a self-assembled multivalent photoaffinity probe and utilized it to capture histone Kcr reader (
32
) and Khib erasers (
33
). In this study, we further designed the probe and integrated it with quantitative proteomics approach to interrogate binders of histone lactylation. Employing this strategy, we determined the interactomes of lactylation of H3 lysine 14 (H3K14la), a histone mark correlated with cervical cancer (CC) and identified DPF2 as a target of this mark. Biochemical and structural studies as well as CUT&Tag analysis verified that DPF2 enables recognition with H3K14la via its DPF domain and associated with it on gene promoters. Disruption of DPF2–H3K14la interaction via structure-based mutation led to the suppressed expression of target genes, including oncogenes that are essential for cell growth and survival. Collectively, our data unravel DPF2 as a H3K14la effector that links histone lactylation to tumorigenesis.
Results
Histone Lactylation Correlates with Cell Proliferation and Tumorigenesis.
Cancer cells often exhibit active glycolysis despite the presence of oxygen, which causes the production of high levels of lactate derived from a metabolic reaction catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (
34
,
35
). The lactate in turn boosts histone lactylation known for its role in epigenetic regulation (
8
,
36
). However, it remains unclear what the function of histone lactylation in the progression of CC. We hypothesized that high LDH levels could lead to a large amount of lactate production, thereby contributing to elevated histone lactylation that may further mediate cervical carcinogenesis.
To test this hypothesis, we first analyzed the LDH levels using gene expression profiling interactive analysis (GEPIA) and found that LDH was dramatically upregulated in cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma (CESC) as well as uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS) and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) (
Fig. 1
A
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S1
A
and B
). Besides, another key enzyme of glycolysis-pyruvate kinase (PKM) also showed high expression (
SI Appendix, Fig. S1
C
), implying the occurrence of metabolic reprogramming in CC. Moreover, the high level of LDH was associated with short overall survival (
Fig. 1
B
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S1
D
). In contrast, we observed that LDH inhibitor (LDHi) significantly suppressed cell proliferation (
Fig. 1
C
). Together, these data suggest a potential link between increased lactate level and cervical carcinogenesis.

To determine changes in histone lactylation owing to the upregulated expression of LDH resulting from metabolic switch in CC, western blotting analysis of extracted histones as well as cytosolic and nucleoplasm fractions were performed and illustrated an obvious increase in the levels of pan-lysine lactylation (pan-Kla), and in particular H3K14la instead of H3K14ac, in the presence of lactate (
Fig. 1
D
and
E
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S1
E
and F
), suggesting that the cellular lactate could fuel histone lactylation. Besides, we also identified lactyl-CoA that was recognized as donor for histone lactylation from Hela cells and showed that the increase of global lactylation was correlated with the rise of lactyl-CoA level with lactate supplementation (
SI Appendix, Fig. S2
). Of note, we identified H3K14la from Hela cells via LC-MS/MS analysis and revealed that the relative proportion of H3K14la was elevated with lactate pretreatment (
SI Appendix, Fig. S3
). Collectively, these results signified that lactate is a direct determinant of Kla and elevated histone lactylation, especially H3K14la, may result in CC tumorigenesis and progression.
Identification of DPF2 as H3K14la Target using a Chemoproteomic Approach.
Given that hPTMs are commonly served as docking sites for the recognition of reader proteins to transduce molecular signals and downstream outcomes, it is reasonable to speculate that H3K14la may recruit its candidate binders to mediate specific gene transcription and tumorigenesis. Besides, we envision that a chemical proteomics strategy relying on multivalent photoaffinity probe as well as quantitative proteomics enables to facilitate the elucidation of hPTM targets. We then developed probe H3K14la consisting of multivalent Kla-deposited peptide (mimic histone Kla) along with photo-cross-linker linked polyethylene glycol (PEG) through a self-assembled technique as described in our previous work (
32
), improving the labeling and capture of H3K14la target proteins. The probe was then synthesized and confirmed by mass spectrometry (
SI Appendix, Fig. S4
). In addition, we also prepared probe H3K14, which contains K instead of Kla, but is otherwise identical to probe H3K14la (
Fig. 2
A
).

We next employed the probes to unravel H3K14la effectors by leveraging a label-free, comparative proteomics experiments (
37
,
38
), in which probes H3K14la and H3K14 were incubated with nuclear extracts, respectively, and triggered photo-cross-linking under UV irradiation. Through ruling out nonspecific binding proteins by stringent washing, the labeled proteins were isolated with centrifugation, followed by on-bead digestion and quantitative LC-MS/MS detection (
Fig. 2
A
and
Dataset S1
). Proteins that showed significantly enriched [averaged fold change > 1.5,
P
-value < 0.05 (n = 3)] over the control probe H3K14 were sorted as candidate H3K14la interactors (
Fig. 2
B
).
In total, 170 protein candidates meeting the above criteria were obtained, and the gene ontology (GO) analysis on these targets illustrated that most of them were involved in diverse functional classes, including RNA binding, protein kinase, and transcription (
Fig. 2
C
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S5
A
and B
). Intriguingly, we also identified the erasers for the removal of histone lactylation (HDAC3) (
39
) as well as the writers responding for the decoration of Kla (KAT5) (
40
), corroborating the advantage of our approach for capturing transient interactions mediated by hPTMs. Importantly, several candidates related to transcription were observed, suggesting that these proteins may be recognized by H3K14la to regulate gene expression. Among them, DPF2 is a subunit of the BAF chromatin remodeling complexes that implicated in cancers and has been found to be recognized by histone acetylation and crotonylation (
41
,
42
). Of note, our probe indeed identified DPF2 as a potential H3K14la binder (
SI Appendix, Fig. S5
C
and D
), and we therefore anticipate that DPF2 may be recognized by H3K14la to mediate transcription and epigenetic function in cancers.
DPF2 Binds H3K14la through Its DPF Domain In Vitro.
Considering that the double PHD finger (DPF) domain of DPF2 has histone acetylation binding activity (
41
), we next asked whether DPF could directly bind to H3K14la in vitro. To this end, we recombinantly expressed DPF domain of DPF2 (DPF2
DPF
) and performed isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) assay using histone H3K14 (1-20) peptides, with binding dissociation constants (Kd) of 0.60 μM, 0.65 μM, and >100 μM for H3K14la, H3K14ac, and unmodified peptides, respectively (
Fig. 3
A
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S6
A
). Notably, we also carried out ITC detection using the expressed DPF domain of DPF1 and DPF3 and found that both appeared nearly complete loss of binding affinity with H3K14la (
SI Appendix, Fig. S6
B
). Together, these results revealed that DPF2 directly and efficiently bound to H3K14la via its DPF domain.

To explore the underlying molecular basis of H3K14la–DPF2
DPF
interactions, we docked the binding of DPF2
DPF
(PDB: 5B79) with H3K14la peptide. The docking analysis revealed that DPF2
DPF
recognized with Kla by adopting a similar Kac-binding model in which the N-terminal a-helix of H3 engaged with the second PHD finger (PHD2) by electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions (such as D346 and L342), while Kla was anchored in a hydrophobic pocket of the first PHD finger (PHD1) (
Fig. 3
C
and
D
and
SI Appendix, Fig S6
C
). The lactylamide moieties of Kla inserts a deep and snug cage constituting some key residues, such as D274, F275, R300, and E326. Of note, the hydroxyl group within Kla interacts with residue D274 through two direct hydrogen bonds that potentiates H3K14la–DPF2 recognition, highlighting a recognition mechanism of Kla that distinct from Kac (
Fig. 3
E
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S6
D
and E
).
To further determine the contribution of key H3K14la-binding residues, we implemented mutagenesis and ITC experiments. Structure-guided mutagenesis was designed to alanine mutation of the Kla pocket residues including D274, R300, as well as D346 that engages in PHD1. Consequently, the ITC assay demonstrated that all the mutations caused a dramatic affinity drop by comparison of wide-type (WT) DPF2
DPF
. Collectively, these findings indicate that DPF2 may recognize H3K14la through its DPF domain via some key residues like D274.
DPF2 Is Intracellular Associated with H3K14la.
To test the association between DPF2 and H3K14la in cells, we overexpressed Flag-tagged DPF2 (WT-DPF2) as well as its mutants (Mut) including DPF2–D274A and DPF2–D274A–R300A in Hela cells, respectively, and tested whether the Flag-DPF2-based pulldown was dependent on DPF2–H3K14la interactions. The chromatin was extracted from the cells and subjected to immunoprecipitation (IP) using anti-Flag beads (
Fig. 4
A
). The following immunoblotting analysis by anti-H3K14la antibody revealed that lactylated histone H3 were indeed trapped by WT-DPF2 rather than its mutants (
Fig. 4
B
), corroborating the association of DPF2 with H3K14la in cells.

We further performed immunofluorescence (IF) assay to assess their colocalization in cells transfected by WT-DPF2 or its mutants. The cells were reacted with antibodies against Flag and H3K14la, and the representative images were displayed in
Fig. 4
C
. Consequently, the signals resulting from WT-DPF2 and H3K14la were merged with a high pearson correlation coefficient of 0.77, thereby confirming their colocalization in cells. In contrast, the value of DPF2 mutants dropped significantly compared with WT-DPF2 (
Fig. 4
D
), indicating the disruption of H3K14la–DPF2 colocalization due to mutations. Taken together, these results infer that DPF2 may be related to H3K14la in cells.
DPF2 Colocalizes with H3K14la Across Genome and Mediates Gene Transcription.
To test whether DPF2 couples with H3K14la on native chromatin, we performed CUT&Tag assays in Hela cells with lactate pretreatment. The cells stably expressing Flag-tagged DPF2 were immunoprecipitated via antibodies against Flag or H3K14la, followed by high-throughput sequencing analysis. In total, we identified 1803 H3K14la-enriched peaks and 9747 DPF2-binding peaks, representing a wide distribution across the genome (
Fig. 5
A
) and implicating that DPF2 may not only be recruited to chromatin by H3K14la. Specifically, 1,037 gene peaks were co-occupied by both H3K14la and DPF2 that accounts for 58% of H3K14la-bound peaks, among which numerous peaks were harbored within gene promoter regions (23.4%) as well as other intergenic regions like enhancers (
Fig. 5
B
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
A
). Furthermore, the heatmap plotting analysis showed that both H3K14la and DPF2 were enriched at transcription start sites (TSSs) and adjacent regions (
Fig. 5
C
), suggesting that DPF2 may correlate with H3K14la for the regulation of gene transcription. Besides, GO analysis revealed that the overlapped genes were involved in vital biological processes, including regulation of cell proliferation, cell migration, and cell signaling (
Fig. 5
D
). By contrast, we applied GO analysis for the peaks co-occupied by H3K14ac and DPF2 and showed that the overlapped genes are implicated in various processes distinguished from H3K14la, suggesting that H3K14la may deposit on genes distinct from H3K14ac (
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
B
). To further determine whether the colocalization of DPF2 and H3K14la is dependent on BAF complex, we performed CUT&Tag assay using an anti-Flag antibody against Flag-BAF47 (one component of BAF complex) and found that BAF47 was highly occupied with the overlapped peaks of DPF2 and H3K14la, demonstrating that H3K14la was recognized by DPF2 in a BAF complex-dependent manner across genome (
SI Appendix, Fig. S8
). Genome browser views of the CUT&Tag signals of a subset of genes involved in cell proliferation and tumorigenesis, such as SEMA5A, ROCK1, and SOAT1, further corroborated the co-occupancy of DPF2 and H3K14la in TSSs (
Fig. 5
F
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
C
). Intriguingly, H3K14ac-marked gene signals showed pronounced decrease compared with H3K14la (such as ROCK1 and SOAT1) (
Fig. 5
F
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
D
), which may imply that lactate boosts H3K14la, that in turn competes with H3K14ac, thereby specifically mediates gene transcription in a manner differed from histone acetylation.

We next asked whether the DPF2-occupied peaks are enriched in a DPF-domain-dependent manner, stable cells expressing Mut-DPF2 were established, and CUT&Tag determination was implemented. Expectedly, the average occupancies of Mut-DPF2 in promoter regions were significantly lowered compared with WT-DPF2 (
Fig. 5
E
), which indicates that the DPF domain is essential for DPF2-bound on chromatin. In line with this, we also observed the attenuated signals of target genes (e.g., SEMA5A) resulting from the Mut-DPF2 (
Fig. 5
F
and
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
C
).
On the basis of our findings that the correlation between DPF2 and H3K14la at promoter regions and lactate boosts H3K14la instead of H3K14ac, we propose that DPF2–H3K14la recognition confer transcription, and the genes modulated by this recognition could be obtained through a quantitative RNA-Seq analysis of cells expressing WT-DPF2 and Mut-DPF2 prior to lactate supplementation. To assess this, we performed RNA-Seq detection from WT-DPF2 or Mut-DPF2 expressed cells upon lactate pre-treatment. Our analysis of the results revealed that more than 600 genes were downregulated owing to the DPF2 mutation, and majority of them were related to regulation of cell survival, adhesion, and so on (
SI Appendix, Fig. S7
E
and F
). Notably, we did find that DPF2 mutation led to significant suppressed expression of the selected oncogenes, despite the presence of lactate. Besides, lactate rather than acetate pretreatment in cells expressing DPF2 boosts transcription, and lactate promotes H3K14la but not H3K14ac (
Fig. 1
D
), indicating that H3K14la instead of H3K14ac contributes to the activation of these genes (
Fig. 5
G
). Overall, these data demonstrated that DPF2 might recognize the H3K14la mark at promoters to mediate gene transcription in a DPF-domain-dependent manner.
DPF2 Links Histone Lactylation to Cell Survival.
Encouraged by our results that DPF2 interacts with H3K14la to regulate transcription of genes implicated with cancer, we next explored whether this association would promote cancer cell growth and survival. For this purpose, CCK-8 detection as well as colony formation assay were performed using cells under lactate feeding, and the results were displayed in
Fig. 6
. We observed that depletion of DPF2 did cause remarkable reduction of cell proliferation and colony forming capability despite in the presence of lactate, suggesting that H3K14la may function mainly through recognition of DPF2. However, the ectopic expression of WT-DPF2, but not its mutants, enabled to restore this reduction (
Fig. 6
A
–
D
). Besides, the BAF complex proteins captured by WT-DPF2 and Mut-DPF2 from Hela cells have no obvious difference (
SI Appendix, Fig. S10
), suggesting that DPF2 mutation did not affect BAF complex stabilization. Furthermore, we performed CCK-8 and colony formation assay in the presence or absence of lactate and found that lactate supplementation did promote H3K14la as well as cell growth, which indicates H3K14la contributes to cell survival (
SI Appendix, Fig. S9
). These findings indicate that the recognition of DPF2 by H3K14la contributes to cell growth and survival through promoting oncogenesis-related genes expression. Taken together, our study supports a potential model wherein DPF2 recognizes histone lactylation and correlates with it at target gene promoters thereafter recruits transcriptional apparatus to chromatin, driving cancer-associated genes expression and tumor cell proliferation, whereas disruption of the H3K14la–DPF2 interaction via DPF domain mutation or the reduction in histone lactylation by LDH restriction impaired cell survival (
Fig. 6
E
).

Discussion
The Warburg effect occurs in most cancers, in which elevated levels of lactate were produced. In addition to being a metabolite, lactate serves as a substrate for histone lactylation, a novel mark that links metabolism and employs pivotal roles in diverse diseases like cancer (
43
–
45
). However, the underlying mechanism of histone lactylation associated with CC remains to be explored. In this study, we demonstrated that CC underwent metabolic rewiring where histone lactylation, particularly H3K14la, was boosted owing to LDH upregulation and lactate accumulation, which in turn foster cell proliferation and survival.
In light of the facts that histone PTM could be recognized by reader proteins for the regulation of gene transcription and functional outputs, we thus sought to dissect the candidate protein effectors of H3K14la using a multivalent photoaffinity probe. In combination with a quantitative proteomics approach, we identified DPF2 as a bona fide target of H3K14la. The following biochemical and molecular docking studies inferred that DPF2 binds to H3K14la via its DPF domain where the key residue-D274 directly interacts with Kla through hydrogen bond, that differs from Kac, for stabilizing the recognition. Although serving as a histone acetylation reader, DPF2 used a distinct binding mode for reading of Kla, which may support the alternative outputs of histone lactylation in responses to certain circumstances. Further CUT&Tag and RNA-Seq analysis revealed that Mut-DPF2 leads to the disruption of H3K14la–DPF2 interaction at gene promoters, thereby alleviating the expression of several oncogenes and cell survival. We thus envision that an inhibitor-specific targeting D274 residue of DPF would perturb the recruitment of DPF2 onto chromatin and synergize the BRD4 inhibition-induced suppression of target genes in CC. The “inhibitor” may be explored as a promising therapeutic option.
This work unravels a putative mechanism in which histone lactylation recognizes with DPF2 and thereby mediates oncogenes transcription in cancer cells. Whether this mechanism acts in other models including cancer metastasis, chemoresistance, and DNA damage repair, could be assessed in further investigations. In addition to fueling histone lactylation, elevated LDL expression or lactate supplement may also promote Kla modification on other proteins associated with cancers. Future studies are desired to evaluate the potential role of lactylation on “other proteins” in orchestrating cell survival. Besides, we detected the binding capacity of DPF2 and histone lactylation by using ITC assay via DPF domain and H3K14la peptide, which represents a reductionist approach and overlooks a fact that H3K14la recruits DPF2 depending on the BAF complex, which in turn interacts with histones through its other components.
In conclusion, our work unveils DPF2 as a protein effector of histone lactylation that are previously unexplored. Furthermore, we contribute a candidate mechanism that DPF2 is recruited to H3K14la-marked chromatin regions for gene regulation. We envision that our study may provide an opportunity to understand the epigenetic regulatory mechanisms underlying histone lactylation.
Materials and Methods
Materials.
Deacetylase inhibitor Cocktail (100X) (P1112) was obtained from Beyotime and protease inhibitor cocktail (100X) (C0001) was obtained from Roche. Primary antibodies were obtained from PTM BIO [Kla (PTM-1401RM), H3K14ac (PTM-113RM), H3K14la (PTM-1414RM), H3K9la (PTM-1419RM), H3K18la (PTM-1406RM), H4K5la (PTM-1407RM), H4K8la (PTM-1415RM)], Cell Signaling Technology [Histone H3, (96C10)], and Sigma-Aldrich [FLAG M2, (F3165)]. Sodium L-lactate (71718) and sodium oxamate (O2751) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Histone peptides with and without lysine lactylation (Kla) modification were synthesized and HPLC purified by Beijing SciLight Biotechnology Ltd. Co. Thiolated polyethylene glycol (HS-PEG) modified with benzophenone (HS-PEG-Bpa) was obtained from ToYong Biotech Ltd. AuNPs was purchased from BBI solutions. HPLC solvents used for mass spectrometric analysis of proteins were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific Ltd.
Enrichment of Endogenous Binding Proteins using Probe H3K14la.
Briefly, 2 mM H3K14la peptides and 1 mM HS-PEG-Bpa were mixed and added to the solution of gold nanoparticles (200 μL), and the mixture was shaken at room temperature for 12 h. Then, the functionalized gold nanoparticles were washed with H

The functionalized probes H3K14la and H3K14 were, respectively, incubated with 0.5 mg of nuclear extracts for 12 h at 4 °C in a rotation wheel. Then, the mixture was irradiated at 365 nm on ice for 20 min using UVP Crosslinker (Analytik Jena). After centrifugation, the precipitation was washed twice with wash buffer 1 (4 M urea in PBS), followed by once washing with buffer 2 (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8, 200 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 1 mM ZnCl
2
) and one wash with wash buffer 3 (100 mM NH
4

3
). Next, the pellet was suspended in 50 μL NH
4

(100 mM) and digested with trypsin at 37 °C overnight. The resulting solution was centrifuged for 2 min and the supernatant was collected. Then, 5 mM DTT was added and incubated with the obtained solution for 1 h, followed by reaction with 15 mM iodoacetamide and 30 mM cysteine at room temperature. The resulting peptide mixture was desalted with C18 material and further analyzed by HPLC-MS/MS.
Immunofluorescence Assay.
For immunofluorescent staining, cells were grown on chamber slides, washed in PBS, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. After fixing, the cells were then permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS, blocked by 10% normal goat serum (NGS), and then incubated with anti-FLAG (F3165, Sigma-Aldrich) and H3K14la (PTM-1414RM, PTMBio) antibodies for 12 h at 4 °C. Next, cells were incubated with Alexa Fluor–conjugated secondary antibodies for 1.5 h in room temperature. Finally, the cells were counterstained with DAPI and imaged using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (Zeiss LSM 900). All images were subsequently analyzed using ImageJ.
CUT&Tag.
CUT&Tag was performed using the Hyperactive Universal CUT&Tag Assay Kit for Illumina (TD903, Vazyme Biotech) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, HeLa cells expressing Flag-WT-DPF2 or its mutants, and cells expressing Flag-WT-BAF47 were collected and counted for incubation with pre-coated concanavalin A beads. Subsequently, cells were permeabilized by digitonin and incubated with Flag or H3K14la antibodies. Next, the samples were incubated with pA-Tn5 transposase. After transposon activation and tagmentation, DNA was isolated, amplified, and purified to construct library. The samples were then analyzed on an Illumina NovaSeq 150PE platform.
RNA-seq Analysis.
Total RNA was extracted from HeLa cells by TRIzol (Invitrogen) and were then sequenced using the Illumina Hiseq 2500. The raw reads were mapped to the human reference genome (hg19) and transcriptome using the RNA-Seq unified mapper. Read counts for each transcript were calculated using HTseq v0.6.1 using default parameters 54. Differential gene expression analyses were performed using the “exactTest” function in edgeR v3.055.
Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) Assay.
CCK-8 was used to measure cell proliferation. HeLa cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 2,000 cells per well. After adhesion, the cells were treated with 20 mM sodium lactate or 20 mM sodium oxamate. Every 24 h for 7 d, 10 μL of the CCK-8 solution was added to each well with incubation for 2 h at 37 °C. The absorbance of each well was then measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek). Finally, the numbers of living cells over 7 d were plotted in a graph to calculate the cell proliferation rate.
